title: DFS in Karaköy: Find the route with Deep Search!
description: Watch Depth-First Search (DFS) “dive” through a street-like graph, exploring as far as possible before backtracking. This reel visualizes how DFS navigates real-world map structure to discover a path.
ig_caption:
🧭✨ DFS in Istanbul’s Karaköy (Karaköy vibes, deep exploration mode!)

🔎 Depth-First Search (DFS) picks a neighboring node, keeps going down that path, and only backtracks when it hits a dead end. In graph theory terms, DFS systematically traverses vertices by following adjacency edges—often using a stack (explicit or via recursion). 

🗺️ On a street-map-style graph, intersections become nodes and roads become edges. DFS doesn’t guarantee the shortest route, but it’s powerful for discovering connectivity and building traversal trees—especially when the goal is “find a path” rather than “find the optimal path.”

✅ Want to see different DFS variants (stack-based vs recursive, iterative deepening, or constrained DFS with heuristics)? Comment what you want next 👇

📣 Share this with a friend who loves algorithms—and tell me: would DFS get lost in the streets of Karaköy or find the way fast? 🚦

In this visualization over a street-like map graph (intersections as nodes, roads as edges), DFS demonstrates how connectivity and path discovery work—even when the first path found isn’t the shortest.

yt_description:
DFS VISUALIZATION in Istanbul (Karaköy)! 🚀 Depth-First Search (DFS) explores a graph by going deep first, then backtracking. In this video, we map real-world-style streets to a graph (nodes=intersections, edges=roads) and show how DFS finds a path through adjacency relationships.

Keywords: DFS, Depth First Search, pathfinding, graph algorithms, algorithms visualization, coding reel, computer science, stack vs recursion.

Mechanics: watch the traversal order, observe backtracking at dead ends, and see the DFS traversal tree grow in real time.
